# Marginalia

A few years ago I bought a used copy of a novel—let me be honest, I don't remember which novel—and found, on page 142, a stranger's handwriting in soft pencil: *"This is exactly what happened with David."* That's all. No date, no name, no elaboration. I have thought about that sentence more than I've thought about whole chapters of the book itself. Who was David? What did he do? The stranger read something true enough to sting a little, and reached for a pencil, and told the margin.

This is the strange afterlife of books: they accumulate people. A book is printed in identical thousands, and then life gets to it. One copy goes to a careful reader who keeps it pristine for forty years. Another goes to someone who reads in the bathtub, in the rain, over spaghetti. Another becomes a record of arguments—"No!" in the margin, "yes, but consider—," exclamation points like little flags planted on the sentences that mattered.

The monks who copied medieval manuscripts knew this. In cold scriptoria they wrote the same sacred texts for months at a time, and in the margins they told the truth about it. "Writing is excessive drudgery," one scribe confessed. "It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." Another wrote simply, "Thank God it will soon be dark." There are manuscripts with inky cat paw prints walking across the page—some monk's companion strolled through wet ink six hundred years ago and is still walking. There are knights in the margins doing battle with snails, and nobody knows why. The scholars have theories; the snails keep their counsel.

And then there are the manicules: little pointing hands drawn by readers to mark the passages that mattered, some of them astonishingly elaborate, with ruffled cuffs and extended index fingers, reaching across centuries to say: *here, look at this, this is the good part.*

The most famous margin note in history was written by Pierre de Fermat, who in 1637 was reading his copy of Diophantus and scribbled that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of a certain theorem—but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years proving him right. Either way you read it, the man weaponized a margin. He turned the white space at the edge of a page into a cliffhanger that outlasted everyone who first puzzled over it.

Readers divide, I've found, into two tribes: those who write in books and those who would sooner write on a human face. The second tribe believes a book is an object of reverence, and our passing thoughts have no business interrupting the author's best ones. The first believes that an unmarked book is a conversation the reader refused to have. Coleridge—who actually coined the English word "marginalia"—belonged so completely to the first tribe that his friends would lend him books hoping he'd annotate them; the scribbled-in copies came back worth more than they left. Mark Twain's margins are full of magnificent rage. And on Robben Island, prisoners passed around a smuggled copy of Shakespeare's complete works disguised as a religious text, and each man signed his name beside a passage. Nelson Mandela chose lines from *Julius Caesar*: "Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once." That book—signatures in the margins, names laid against poetry—is now one of the great artifacts of its century, and it's an artifact precisely because someone wrote in it.

Anne Fadiman distinguishes between courtly and carnal love of books: the courtly lover keeps the book perfect, at a worshipful distance; the carnal lover breaks spines, dog-ears pages, gets soup on chapter three, and considers all of it devotion. I think she's right that it's love either way—but only one way leaves evidence.

Which raises a genuinely modern question: where have the margins gone? E-books can be highlighted, certainly, and your device will even show you "popular highlights"—passages underlined by thousands of strangers, a crowd's manicule. But it isn't the same, and the difference isn't nostalgia. Marginalia were slow and specific and slightly inconvenient, which is exactly why they were honest. Nobody ever penciled *"This is exactly what happened with David"* because an app suggested it. The friction was the point. A margin note had to be worth reaching for the pencil.

Underneath the practicality, I don't think marginalia are really notes to a future self. They're messages in an uncertain direction—to the book, to the author, to whoever picks the thing up next, to nobody. A way of saying *I was here*—and more than that: *I was here and I was changed, briefly, by the eleventh sentence on page 142.* Reading feels solitary, but the margins insist otherwise. Every annotated book is small proof that reading is a relationship—that a page is not a wall but a door, and people keep knocking.

Somewhere out there is a copy of a novel with my handwriting in it, too. I sold it or gave it away years ago, and I can no longer remember what I wrote. I'd like to think someone is on page 142 right now, reading my pencil marks, wondering about me. I hope I gave them something worth wondering about. I hope, at least, that I had the decency to be interesting—to argue with the author, to plant my little flags, to point with a drawn hand at the good part and say to a stranger I'd never meet: *here. Look at this.*

**Marginalia**

A few years ago I bought a used copy of a novel — let me be honest, I don't remember which novel — and found, on page 142, a stranger's handwriting in soft pencil: "This is exactly what happened with David." That's all. No date, no name, no elaboration. I have thought about that sentence more than I have thought about whole chapters of the book itself. Who was David? What did he do? The stranger read something true enough to hurt a little, and reached for a pencil, and told the margin.

This is the strange afterlife of books: they accumulate people. A book is printed in identical thousands, and then life gets to it. One copy goes to a careful reader who keeps it pristine for forty years. Another goes to someone who reads in the bathtub, in the rain, over spaghetti. Another becomes a palimpsest of arguments — "No!" in the margin, "yes but consider—," exclamation points like little flags planted on the sentences that mattered.

The people who copyedited medieval manuscripts knew this. Monks in cold scriptoria wrote the same sacred texts for months at a time, and in the margins they told the truth about it. "Writing is excessive drudgery," one scribe confessed. "It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." Another wrote simply, "Thank God it will soon be dark." There are manuscripts with inky cat paw prints walking across the page — some monk's companion strolled through wet ink six hundred years ago and is still walking. There are knights in the margins doing battle with snails, and nobody knows why. The scholars have theories; the snails keep their counsel.

And then there are the manicules: little pointing hands, drawn by readers to mark the passages that mattered, some of them astonishingly elaborate, with ruffled cuffs and extended index fingers, reaching across centuries to say: here, look at this, this is the good part.

The most famous margin note in history was written by Pierre de Fermat, who in 1637 was reading his copy of Diophantus and scribbled that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of a certain theorem — but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians spent 358 years proving him right, or proving that he was probably bluffing, depending on your view. Either way, the man weaponized a margin. He turned the white space at the edge of a page into a cliffhanger that outlasted everyone who first puzzled over it.

Readers divide, I've found, into two tribes: those who write in books and those who would sooner write on a human face. The second group believes a book is an object of reverence, that the printed word is the author at their best, and that our passing thoughts have no business interrupting. The first group believes that a book unread-in is a conversation the reader refused to have. Coleridge — who actually coined the English word "marginalia" — belonged so completely to the first tribe that his friends would lend him books in the hope that he'd annotate them; the scribbled-in copies came back worth more than they left. Mark Twain's margins are full of magnificent rage. And on Robben Island, prisoners passed around a smuggled copy of Shakespeare's complete works disguised as a religious text, and each man signed his name beside a passage. Nelson Mandela chose lines from Julius Caesar: "Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once." That book — signatures in the margins, names laid against poetry — is now one of the great artifacts of the century, and it's an artifact precisely because someone wrote in it.

Anne Fadiman distinguishes between courtly love and carnal love of books: the courtly lover keeps the book perfect, at a worshipful distance; the carnal lover breaks spines, dog-ears pages, underlines, gets soup on chapter three, and considers all of it a form of devotion. I think she's right that it's love either way — but only one way leaves evidence.

Which brings me to now, and to a genuine question: where have the margins gone? E-books can be highlighted, certainly, and your device will even show you "popular highlights" — passages underlined by thousands of strangers, a crowd's manicule. But it's not the same, and the difference isn't nostalgia. Marginalia were slow and specific and slightly inconvenient, which is exactly why they were honest. Nobody ever penciled "This is exactly what happened with David" because an app suggested it. The friction was the point. A margin note had to be worth the reaching for the pencil.

I keep thinking about what marginalia really are, underneath the practicality. They're not notes to a future self, mostly. They're messages in a slightly uncertain direction — to the book, to the author, to whoever picks the thing up next, to nobody. They're a way of saying I was here, and more than that: I was here and I was changed, briefly, by sentence eleven on page 142. Reading feels solitary, but the margins insist otherwise. Every annotated book is a small proof that reading is a relationship — that a page is not a wall but a door, and people keep knocking.

Somewhere out there is a copy of a novel with my handwriting in it, too. I sold it or gave it away years ago, and I can no longer remember what I wrote. I'd like to think someone is on page 142 right now, reading my pencil marks, wondering about me. I hope I gave them something worth wondering about. I hope, at least, that I had the decency to be interesting — to argue with the author, to plant my little flags, to point with my drawn hand at the good part and say to a stranger I'd never meet: here. Look at this.
